slides.narration: Welcome. Today we study The Thief’s Story by Ruskin Bond, in which a young thief is changed by a man who trusts him. Please read the story in your textbook, Footprints without Feet, before you go on. This lesson does not repeat the text. In the board exam, this reader is tested through short and long answers on character, theme and values.

slides.heading: How to use this lesson
bullets: Read the story once in *Footprints without Feet*.
Use these slides for the sequence of events, the themes and the two characters.
The board asks 3-mark and 6-mark questions on this reader, not extracts: practise those most.
Explain events **in your own words**; do not memorise lines.
slides.narration: Here is how to use this lesson. Read the story first. Then use these slides for the order of events, the themes and the two characters, Hari and Anil. The board does not print extracts from this reader; it asks short and long answers. So focus on explaining, in your own words, why Hari changes and what Anil’s silence means.

visual.alt: Table of facts: the author is Ruskin Bond, born 1934, an Indian writer known for gentle stories of ordinary people in north India; the story is told in the first person by the thief; it is set in a north Indian town with a railway line to Lucknow; the main characters are Hari Singh, a young thief, and Anil, a young writer.

slides.narration: Ruskin Bond, born in nineteen thirty-four, is one of India’s best-loved writers in English. His stories are gentle and observant, often about ordinary people in small towns and hill stations. This story is told in the first person by the thief himself, so we hear his clever plans and, later, his doubts, directly from him.

slides.heading: The story in six stages
slides.body_md: A theft that is undone, and a change of heart. (A SOYL summary, not the text.)

nodes.label: A wet note and a smile

visual.alt: Flow of the story in six stages: a thief finds a target; food, cooking and lessons; money under the mattress; the theft and the station; thinking in the rain; a wet note and a smile.
visual.caption: The story in six stages (SOYL summary).

slides.narration: The story moves through six stages. A young thief finds a target in Anil. He gets food, cooking practice and lessons. Anil brings home money and hides it under his mattress. Hari steals it and goes to the station. In the rain he thinks again. And the next morning, a wet note and a smile end the story. Keep this map in mind.

slides.heading: Summary 1: a thief finds a target
slides.body_md: The narrator is a young, practised thief who changes his name whenever it suits him; for now he is Hari Singh. He picks out Anil, a young writer, at a wrestling match, flatters him and asks for work. Anil cannot pay wages but offers food if Hari will cook. Hari says he can, which is a lie.
slides.narration: Our narrator is a young thief, experienced at his trade, who changes his name to suit his plans. At present he calls himself Hari Singh. At a wrestling match he spots Anil, a young writer, flatters him and asks for work. Anil cannot pay, but he offers food in return for cooking. Hari claims he can cook, though he cannot.

slides.heading: Summary 2: food, cooking and lessons
slides.body_md: Hari’s first meal is so bad that Anil gives it to a stray dog, yet he teaches the boy to cook. He also teaches him to write his name and promises full sentences and sums. Hari is grateful, but he still keeps a little of the shopping money. Anil, paid irregularly for his writing, hardly notices.
slides.narration: Hari’s first meal is a disaster; Anil hands it to a stray dog. But instead of sending him away, Anil teaches him to cook, then to write his name, and promises to teach him sentences and sums. Hari is grateful, yet he still keeps a little of the shopping money. Anil, who is paid only now and then for his writing, hardly notices.

slides.heading: Check: the order of events
slides.narration: Your turn. Six events from the story are shuffled. Put them in order, from the meeting at the wrestling match to the morning of the wet note.

slides.heading: Summary 3: the theft and the station
slides.body_md: One day Anil sells a book and brings home a bundle of notes, which he puts under his mattress. That night Hari takes the money and hurries to the station to catch a train to Lucknow. But as the train pulls out, he does not get on.
slides.narration: Then comes the test. Anil sells a book and brings home a bundle of notes, which he tucks under his mattress. That night Hari slides the money out and hurries to the station, planning to take a train to Lucknow and vanish. Yet when the train starts to move, something holds him back, and he lets it leave without him.

slides.heading: Summary 4: thinking in the rain
slides.body_md: Wandering in the rain, Hari imagines how Anil will feel: not angry, but sad that his trust was betrayed. He also realises that learning to read and write could make him a respected person, worth more than any stolen money. He goes back and slips the damp notes under the mattress.
slides.narration: Out in the rain, Hari thinks. He imagines Anil waking up, not angry about the money but saddened that the boy he trusted has betrayed him. He also sees that reading and writing could make him a respected person one day, which stolen money never could. So he returns, and quietly slips the damp notes back under the mattress.

slides.heading: Summary 5: a wet note and a smile
slides.body_md: Next morning Anil has made tea. He hands Hari a fifty-rupee note and says he will be paid regularly now. The note is still damp, so Hari knows Anil found out. Anil says only that they will start writing sentences today. Hari smiles, and neither speaks of the theft.
slides.narration: The next morning, Anil has made tea. He gives Hari a fifty-rupee note and says that from now on he will be paid regularly. Hari notices the note is still damp, and realises Anil knows everything. Yet Anil says nothing about it; he simply announces that today they will begin writing sentences. Hari smiles. The theft is never mentioned.

slides.heading: Theme 1: trust and education change a thief
slides.body_md: Two forces work together on Hari.
columns:
**Trust**

- a stranger taken in without questions
- money placed in his hands
- betrayal becomes painful
- silent forgiveness at the end

**Education**

- writing his own name
- the promise of sentences and sums
- a vision of a respected future
- worth more than stolen notes
slides.narration: The central theme is how trust and education change Hari. Trust makes him feel valued, so betraying Anil becomes painful, and silent forgiveness seals the change. Education shows him a future as a respected person, worth more than any stolen money. In answers, show how both forces work on him, especially at the station and in the rain.

slides.heading: A web of themes

rows: Anil’s faith makes betrayal unbearable for Hari.
Writing his name opens a future for Hari.
The wet note and the silence.
Anil teaches instead of dismissing or reporting.
Anil cares little for money and much for people.

visual.alt: Table of six themes with where each appears: trust transforms, education as a way up, conscience, forgiveness without words, kindness over punishment, and people above money.

slides.narration: Around that centre sit other themes. Conscience, which stops Hari boarding the train. Forgiveness without words, in the wet note and the silence. Kindness over punishment, because Anil teaches rather than reports. And people above money, since Anil cares little for wealth and a great deal for people. Each theme can anchor a six mark answer.

slides.heading: Check: Anil’s method today
slides.narration: Check yourself. A teacher finds a student has copied homework, speaks to him privately and offers extra help instead of punishment. Whose approach from the story does this resemble?

slides.heading: Character: Hari’s change
slides.body_md: Show the change with evidence from the beginning and the end.

rows: Changes his name to suit his plans
Smiles openly at the man he wronged
Flatters and lies to get work
Sees Anil as a teacher and friend

visual.alt: Table contrasting Hari at the start and at the end: from changing names, lying and skimming money, and seeing Anil as a target, to smiling openly, returning the money, choosing learning, and seeing Anil as a teacher and friend.

slides.narration: Hari changes more than anyone else in the story. At the start he changes his name, flatters and lies, skims money and sees Anil as a target. By the end he has returned what he took, chosen learning over easy money, and smiles openly at the man he wronged. A good answer traces this journey step by step, with evidence.

slides.heading: Hari’s inner conflict
columns:
**The thief in him**

- sees an easy chance
- takes the notes
- heads for the train

**The learner in him**

- values Anil’s trust
- wants an educated future
- cannot board; returns the money
slides.narration: Your syllabus asks about Hari’s inner conflict. One side of him is the practised thief who sees a chance, takes the notes and heads for the train. The other side is a grateful learner who values Anil’s trust and wants an educated future. The struggle peaks on the platform and in the rain, and the learner wins.

slides.heading: Character: Anil

rows: Feeds a stranger though he cannot pay wages.
Teaches cooking after a disastrous first meal.
Earns irregularly; keeps notes under a mattress.
Lets Hari handle the shopping money.
Says nothing about the theft; pays him and starts the next lesson.

visual.alt: Table of Anil’s traits with evidence: generous, patient, careless with money, trusting and forgiving.

slides.narration: Anil is generous, feeding a stranger he cannot pay. He is patient, teaching cooking after a disastrous first meal. He is careless with money, which makes him an easy target. Above all, he is trusting and forgiving. His silence after the theft is not ignorance; it is a deliberate kindness that lets Hari keep his dignity.

slides.heading: Check: the train
slides.narration: Try this assertion and reason item. Decide whether each statement is true, and then whether the reason really explains the assertion.

slides.heading: Narration and the ending
bullets: **First-person narrator:** we share the thief’s plans and doubts.
**Understatement:** big feelings, few words.
**A telling detail:** the damp note reveals everything without dialogue.
**An open, silent ending:** forgiveness is shown, not spoken.
**Irony:** the robbed man pays the robber the next morning.
slides.narration: How does Bond tell the story? Through the thief’s own voice, so we share his plans and doubts. He uses understatement: big feelings, few words. A single detail, the damp note, reveals the truth without a conversation. The ending is silent and open; forgiveness is shown, not spoken. And there is irony, since the man who was robbed pays the robber.

slides.heading: A telling detail: SOYL’s own examples
slides.body_md: Practise spotting how one small detail can reveal a whole truth. These sentences are SOYL’s own, not from the story:
bullets: *Mother said nothing about the broken vase, but the next day a tube of glue sat on my desk.* — a detail that shows she knew
*The coach handed me the captain’s armband, still warm from his own hand.* — a detail that shows trust passed on
*My friend returned the borrowed book with a new bookmark inside, at the page I had stopped reading.* — a detail that shows care
slides.narration: Here are three sentences of our own. A tube of glue shows that mother knew about the vase. A warm armband shows trust passed on. A bookmark at the right page shows care. In each, one small object speaks louder than words. Now look at how Bond uses the damp note in your textbook in the same way.

slides.heading: Word meanings

rows: the inner sense of right and wrong
deep regret for a wrong done
to praise insincerely to gain favour

visual.alt: Table of word meanings: conscience, remorse, reform, betray, flatter, irregular, redemption and transformation.
visual.caption: Key words for this story with their meanings.

slides.narration: These words will help you write about the story. Conscience is your inner sense of right and wrong. Remorse is deep regret. To reform is to change for the better, and to betray is to break trust. To flatter is to praise insincerely. Irregular means not at fixed times. Redemption is being saved from wrongdoing, and a transformation is a complete change.

slides.heading: Worked example: planning a 6-mark answer
slides.body_md: *Question:* *How do trust and education change Hari?*
bullets: **Stand:** together they turn a thief towards honesty.
**Points + evidence:** Anil’s trust (money in his hands); lessons (his name, the promise of sentences); the station and the rain.
**Turn:** he returns the money; Anil forgives silently.
**Value + conclusion:** kindness reforms better than punishment.

slides.narration: Here is how to plan a six mark answer. Take a stand: together, trust and education turn Hari towards honesty. Give points with evidence: Anil trusts him with money, teaches him his name, and promises more. Then show the turn at the station and in the rain, and the silent forgiveness. Finish with a value: kindness reforms better than punishment.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Hari Singh, a young thief, gets work with Anil, a writer, by flattery and a lie.
Anil feeds him, teaches him to cook and to write his name.
Hari steals Anil’s money but cannot board the train; in the rain he decides to return it.
A damp fifty-rupee note shows Anil knew; he forgives without a word.
Read the story in *Footprints without Feet*; write about it in your own words.

Hari steals Anil’s money but cannot leave, and in the rain he decides to return it. The next morning, a damp note shows that Anil knew, and forgave him without a word. slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: 3-mark answers (40–50 words): point + evidence + explanation.
6-mark answers (100–120 words): stand → 3 points with evidence → value or theme → conclusion.
Facts often confused: Hari never boarded the train; Anil never mentioned the theft; the note was damp from the rain.
For conflict questions, show both sides of Hari and say which wins and why.
Value questions: trust, forgiveness, education, reform without punishment.
slides.narration: Exam tips. In three mark answers, give a point, evidence and a short explanation. In six mark answers, take a stand, give three supported points, and link to a value. Get the facts right: Hari never boarded the train, Anil never mentioned the theft, and the note was damp from the rain. In conflict questions, show both sides of Hari.

sections.heading: 1. About the text and the author
sections.body_md:
**Read the story itself in your textbook, *Footprints without Feet* (NCERT supplementary reader).** This lesson is SOYL's explanation and analysis; it does not reproduce the text.

**Ruskin Bond** (born 1934) is an Indian writer in English, known for gentle, observant stories of ordinary people in the small towns and hills of north India. This story is told in the first person by the thief himself, so we follow his plans and his change of heart from the inside.

sections.heading: 2. Summary (in SOYL’s words)
sections.body_md:
**The target.** A young, practised thief, calling himself Hari Singh, flatters Anil, a young writer, at a wrestling match and asks for work. Anil offers food instead of wages if Hari will cook; Hari falsely says he can.

**Lessons.** Hari’s first meal goes to a stray dog, but Anil teaches him to cook, to write his name, and promises sentences and sums. Hari still keeps a little of the shopping money.

**The theft.** Anil sells a book and puts the money under his mattress. At night Hari takes it and goes to the station to catch a train to Lucknow, but he does not board.

**The return.** In the rain he thinks of Anil’s sadness at broken trust and of the future education could give him. He returns the damp notes.

**The ending.** Next morning Anil gives him a fifty-rupee note, still damp, and promises regular pay. Hari realises Anil knows. Anil only says they will start writing sentences, and Hari smiles.

sections.heading: 3. Themes and message
sections.body_md:
- **Trust transforms:** Anil’s faith makes betrayal unbearable.
- **Education as a way up:** writing his name shows Hari a future.
- **Conscience:** Hari cannot board the train.
- **Forgiveness without words:** the damp note and the silence.
- **Kindness over punishment:** Anil teaches instead of reporting.
- **People above money:** Anil cares little for wealth.

**Message:** trust, kindness and education can reform a wrongdoer more surely than punishment.

key_terms.definition_md: To change a person, especially for the better.

sections.heading: 8. Answering exam questions
sections.body_md:
**How this reader is examined:** the board sets 3-mark short answers (40–50 words; two of three) and a 6-mark long answer (100–120 words) on *Footprints without Feet*. It does not print extracts from this reader; SOYL’s commentary items are comprehension practice only.

**Short answers (3 marks):** point + evidence + explanation.

**Long answers (6 marks):** a clear stand; three points with evidence in your own words; a link to a value or theme; a one-line conclusion. Extrapolation tasks (Anil’s diary, a letter from Hari years later, an assembly speech) must stay consistent with the story.

Re-read the story in *Footprints without Feet* before a test.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Board weight:** Footprints short answers (3 marks, 40–50 words, two of three) and one long answer (6 marks, 100–120 words) (CBSE 2026-27, Section C). No extracts from this reader.

**How marks are awarded:** content (relevant events, accurately used), interpretation (a clear, supported view or value), and expression within the word limit.

**Common mistakes**
1. Saying Hari escaped on the train: he never boarded it.
2. Saying Anil scolded Hari or called the police: he never mentioned the theft.
3. Missing why the note was damp: it was the returned money, soaked in the rain.
4. Forgetting education as a reason for Hari’s return; trust is only half the answer.
5. Quoting lines from memory instead of explaining in your own words.

**Remember:** read the story in your textbook, *Footprints without Feet*.

questions.passage_md: Bond's narrator introduces himself without shame: he is a young thief, practised at his trade, and he uses whatever name suits him at the moment. When we meet him he is calling himself Hari Singh. He picks out Anil, a young writer, in a crowd watching a wrestling match, flatters him and asks for work. Anil admits he cannot pay a wage but offers food in return for cooking. Hari claims he can cook, which is untrue. His first meal is so poor that Anil hands it to a stray dog, yet instead of sending the boy away, Anil patiently teaches him how to cook.

questions.passage_md: Life with Anil gives Hari more than meals. Anil teaches him to write his name and promises to go further, to full sentences and to sums. For a boy who has never been to school, this is a door opening. Hari is grateful, yet old habits survive: he still keeps a little of the shopping money for himself. Anil, who earns his living by writing for magazines, is paid only now and then, borrowing when he is short and spending freely when he is not. He seems hardly to notice money at all, which makes him, from a thief's point of view, an easy target.

children.stem_md: What was the first thing Anil taught Hari to write?

questions.passage_md: The ending is quietly brilliant. Next morning Anil has already made tea, and he hands Hari a fifty-rupee note, saying that he will pay him regularly from now on. Hari notices that the note is still damp from the rain, and he understands at once: Anil knows about the theft. Yet Anil says nothing of it. This morning

A strange night. When I woke, I reached under my mattress and found the notes there, but they were damp, though no rain could have reached them indoors. Hari must have taken them and gone out into the storm, and then he came back. I felt a stab of hurt that he had stolen from me, but a much greater joy that he had returned. Dear Anil,

I write to you today with a pen you first taught me to hold. When I came to you, I was a thief who lied about cooking and kept some of your shopping money. Today I want to talk about why education is the best reform. In Ruskin Bond’s story, Hari Singh is a young thief who has never been to school. questions.stem_md: What was Anil’s occupation in *The Thief’s Story*?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** a writer. Anil earned his living by writing.

questions.stem_md: What lie did Hari tell Anil when he asked for work?

options.text_md: that he had a family nearby

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** that he could cook. He falsely claimed he could cook.

questions.stem_md: Why did Hari consider Anil an easy person to rob?

options.text_md: Anil was often away for weeks.
Anil was very old and weak.
Anil was trusting and careless about money.
Anil kept his money in the street.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Anil was trusting and careless about money. His trust and casual attitude to money made theft easy.

questions.stem_md: Where did Hari go immediately after taking the money from under Anil’s mattress?

options.text_md: to the bazaar to spend it

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** to the railway station. He hurried to the station to catch a train.

questions.stem_md: Which reason best explains why Hari returned the stolen money?

options.text_md: He valued Anil’s trust and the chance of an education.
He was afraid the police were following him.
The money turned out to be fake.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** He valued Anil’s trust and the chance of an education. Trust and the promise of learning outweighed the money.

questions.stem_md: What did the wet note tell Hari the next morning?

options.text_md: It had rained inside the room.
Anil had been out all night.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Anil knew about the theft. It showed Anil had found the returned, rain-soaked money.

questions.stem_md: Which quality of Anil does the ending of *The Thief’s Story* reveal most clearly?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** forgiveness. He forgives without a word.

questions.stem_md: Which message does *The Thief’s Story* most strongly convey?

options.text_md: Trust and kindness can reform a wrongdoer.
Thieves can never change their ways.
Money is the key to happiness.
Writers are poor judges of character.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Trust and kindness can reform a wrongdoer. Anil’s trust and kindness transform Hari.

questions.stem_md: A teacher finds that a student has copied homework, speaks to him privately and offers extra help instead of punishing him. Whose approach in *The Thief’s Story* does this resemble?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Anil’s. Like Anil, the teacher chooses trust and help over punishment.

questions.stem_md: What is ironic about the ending of *The Thief’s Story*?

options.text_md: The thief is caught by the police.
The victim rewards the thief with wages the morning after the theft.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The victim rewards the thief with wages the morning after the theft. Instead of punishment, Anil pays Hari, the very morning after being robbed.

questions.stem_md: What is the tone of *The Thief’s Story*?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** quiet, warm and reflective. Bond’s tone is gentle and reflective.

questions.stem_md: Who narrates *The Thief’s Story*?

options.text_md: the thief, in the first person

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** the thief, in the first person. Hari Singh, the thief, tells his own story.

questions.stem_md: In *The Thief’s Story*, the young thief was calling himself Hari ___.
questions.solution_md: He used the name Hari **Singh**.

questions.stem_md: Hari’s first meal was so bad that Anil gave it to a stray ___.
questions.solution_md: A stray **dog** got the meal.

questions.stem_md: Anil taught Hari to write his ___ and promised to teach him full sentences and ___.
questions.solution_md: First his **name**, then sentences and **sums**.

questions.stem_md: Next morning Anil gave Hari a fifty-rupee note that was still ___ from the rain.
questions.solution_md: The note was still **wet**.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Hari did not board the train after stealing Anil’s money.

**Reason (R):** Hari’s conscience and his attachment to Anil held him back.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Anil reported the theft to the police.

**Reason (R):** Anil discovered that his money had been taken and returned.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A is false: Anil said nothing to anyone. R is true: the wet note shows he knew.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Anil earned money only now and then.

**Reason (R):** Anil taught Hari to write his name.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both are true, but teaching Hari does not explain Anil’s irregular income, which came from writing for magazines.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Anil had to teach Hari how to cook.

**Reason (R):** Hari had worked as a cook in a hotel before he met Anil.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true. R is false: Hari had lied about cooking; nothing in the story says he had ever worked as a cook.

questions.stem_md: True or false: in *The Thief’s Story*, Anil paid Hari good wages from his first day.
questions.solution_md: **False.** Anil could offer only food at first; regular pay came at the end.

questions.stem_md: True or false: Hari boarded the train to Lucknow with Anil’s money.
questions.solution_md: **False.** He let the train leave without him.

questions.stem_md: True or false: Hari put the stolen notes back under Anil’s mattress.
questions.solution_md: **True.** He returned them before Anil woke.

questions.stem_md: True or false: Anil scolded Hari angrily for the theft the next morning.
questions.solution_md: **False.** Anil never mentioned the theft.

questions.stem_md: Arrange these events of *The Thief’s Story* in the order in which they happen.

options.text_md: Anil gives Hari a wet fifty-rupee note.
Anil brings home money from selling a book.
Anil teaches Hari to cook and to write his name.
Hari returns and puts the money back.
Hari approaches Anil at a wrestling match.
Hari takes the notes and goes to the station.

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (e) → (c) → (b) → (f) → (d) → (a). Meeting → lessons → the money → the theft → the return → the wet note.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: Arrange the stages of Hari’s night after the theft in *The Thief’s Story*.

options.text_md: He lets the train leave without him.
Hari slides the notes from under the mattress.
He slips the damp notes back into place.
He wanders in the rain, thinking.
He waits at the station for the train.

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (b) → (e) → (a) → (d) → (c). Theft → waiting → hesitation → reflection → return.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: Match each item from *The Thief’s Story* with its part in the story.
questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(s), (b)–(q), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). Characters and key objects of the story.

questions.stem_md: Match these words useful for discussing *The Thief’s Story* with their meanings.

match_right.text_md: deep regret for a wrong done
the inner sense of right and wrong

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(s), (b)–(r), (c)–(q), (d)–(p). Key words for writing about this story.

questions.stem_md: Match each action in *The Thief’s Story* with the quality it reveals.

options.text_md: Anil teaches Hari after the bad meal
Hari keeps part of the shopping money
Anil says nothing about the theft

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(q), (d)–(s). Each action and what it shows.
